items.title: Finality is like the speed of light to LLMs from the labs
items.summary: I think you've all noticed the "one more thing" with AI, and the many articles to fix it, and that they don't really fix anything at all. If your task ends, so does token spend, so if you ask an LLM to draw a square (metaphor for a moderately complex system), it will forever draw you an approximation of a square, and after stopping it will always tell you that there is still more work to do. Not matter how much you try to force it to finish it just does not. As if physically it can approach but never reach finality. What has been your experience? Has it improved? How?

items.title: Shirudo doesn't work, this does
items.summary: Great launch....bad product? Why did they announce this CVE patch system without it being ready, at all. Borkmann made a lot of really unique(?) choices in his architecture of this programmable ebpf firewall. It feels relatively unusable today, which I guess they said as much in the docs. Here is a proper version of what they are trying to do. It works right now. Sits on the nic, xdp speed, and you can make the patches yourself if you want. It resets requests carrying the one base64 shape that reaches the bug. eBPF is the right way to do this, probably the only way realistically.

items.title: SimDrop – Running iOS simulators in the macOS Finder sidebar
items.summary: Hi HN, I made a small macOS utility for my own iOS simulator workflow. I kept running into two annoyances: getting config files in and out of a simulator is clunky (digging into CoreSimulator UUID folders or running simctl), and on the iPhone Duo simulator I couldn't even drag and drop images onto the window at all. SimDrop puts every running iOS simulator in Finder's sidebar (under Locations) with two folders: - Downloads/ (Files app > On My iPhone > Downloads) - Photos and Videos/ (the simulator's Photos library) Simulators appear when they boot and disappear when they shut down.

items.title: Tool: npkill
items.summary: Dev env disk cleaner. What we like: Finds dev directories e.g. node_modules, caches, build artifacts, taking up disk space and helps you clear them. Fast TUI with search. Understands language ecosystems for finding relevant locations. Filter by age and specific exclusions. Has an API for integration into your own scripts. What we dislike: Good candidate for shipping as a compiled binary.

items.title: Tool: Voiden
items.summary: Git-native API client. What we like: API request templates live in Git. Docs, requests, examples can all live in the same executable file. API tests can be documented and executed in CI. Has a visual API request builder GUI. Works cross-platform with binary download and OS packages. Good plugin ecosystem. What we dislike: Based on Electron, although they own that decision and explain it well in their docs.
